title: Eat the gruel or shoo the flies?
literal_meaning: Eat the gruel, or shoo the flies?
explanation: A meal is ready, but the flies will not leave it alone. The question catches the frustration of two necessary tasks demanding attention at once: attending to one interrupts the other. It gives that predicament a small, comic scene rather than blaming someone for not doing everything at the same time. The dictionary explicitly applies the saying to two unavoidable tasks arising together.
meaning_odia: ଜାଉ ଖାଇବାକୁ ବସିଛି, ହେଲେ ମାଛି ଘଉଡ଼ାଇବାରୁ ଫୁରୁସତ୍ ନାହିଁ। ଖାଇବା ବି ଦରକାର, ମାଛି ହଟାଇବା ବି ଦରକାର; ଗୋଟିକରେ ମନ ଦେଲେ ଅନ୍ୟଟି ବାଧା ଦେଉଛି। ଏକା ସମୟରେ ଦୁଇଟି ଜରୁରୀ କାମ ପଡ଼ିଲେ କାହାକୁ ଆଗ କରିବା, ସେହି ଅଡ଼ୁଆକୁ ଏହି ଛୋଟ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନଟି ହସ ସହିତ କହେ। ଅଭିଧାନର ଟୀକାରେ ମଧ୍ୟ ଏକା ସମୟର ଦୁଇଟି ଅନିବାର୍ଯ୍ୟ କାର୍ଯ୍ୟ ପାଇଁ ଏହାର ବ୍ୟବହାର ଦିଆଯାଇଛି।
english_summary: Two necessary tasks can compete for the same moment of attention.
odia_summary: ଏକା ବେଳେ ଦୁଇଟି ଜରୁରୀ କାମ ପଡ଼ିଲେ କାହାକୁ ଆଗ କରିବା?
usage_example: At a small event, the person serving lunch is also asked to check arriving guests against a list. They use the question with a laugh and ask another volunteer to take one task. (Original imagined example, not collected testimony.)
cultural_context: Jau is a grain gruel. The printed dictionary pictures flies, not fish; the online Wiktionary transcription drops the final vowel sign in that word. The meal scene and application above expand the dictionary’s stated two-task gloss. No particular household, occupational custom or originating incident is established.
